items.question: How many people who took the 2026 customer survey fall into the Trail Starters segment?
items.content:
### Answer

The evidence does not establish how many 2026 survey respondents fall into the Trail Starters segment [inference]. It contains only individual survey rows, all tagged Trail Starters, and no segment total or total sample size [inference].

### Key findings

- These rows appear to be a subset of a larger file; the row locators reach at least "Row 583" [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R583]], which suggests more rows exist than were provided.

### Conflicting evidence

- The flagged "nps" differences (e.g. 10 in [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R364]] versus 4 in [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R138]]) are ordinary variation between individual respondents, not a conflict about the segment size. They do not bear on the question.

### Interpretation

At least 12 Trail Starters respondents exist, since 12 distinct rows carry that label, but this is a floor based on the sample provided, not a count of the segment [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence gives no segment-level count, total respondent count, or survey methodology summary [inference]. A survey summary report, data dictionary, or the full respondent-level dataset filtered by segment would close the gap.

items.question: Across the full product review export, how many reviews awarded a single star?
items.content:
### Answer

The evidence does not establish how many reviews in the full export awarded a single star. Only a handful of individual review rows are provided, not the full export or any aggregate rating distribution, and none of the rows shown carries a 1-star rating [inference].

### Key findings

- The review rows provided carry ratings of 5 [[NORTHSTAR/REVIEWS@v1:R270]], 4 [[NORTHSTAR/REVIEWS@v1:R555]], 3 [[NORTHSTAR/REVIEWS@v1:R631]], and 3 [[NORTHSTAR/REVIEWS@v1:R322]]; none of these is a single-star rating.
- Review IDs run up to RV-00752 [[NORTHSTAR/REVIEWS@v1:R753]], which suggests an export larger than the sample provided, but the evidence does not state the export's total size or its rating distribution.

### Conflicting evidence

- Review text in several rows says "Three stars feels fair" even where the stated rating differs, for example a rating of 5 in [[NORTHSTAR/REVIEWS@v1:R270]] and a rating of 4 in [[NORTHSTAR/REVIEWS@v1:R555]]. This is an internal inconsistency within the review data, so the text should not be used to infer ratings.

### Gaps & unknowns

The full product review export, or a summary of its rating distribution, is not provided, so a count of single-star reviews cannot be determined. A complete export file, or a pivot or aggregate of ratings by star level, would close this gap. The sampled rows cannot be extrapolated to the full export, since their selection method is unknown.

items.question: What percentage of Southpeak's survey sample chose fit inconsistency as their top issue?
items.content:
### Answer

33% of surveyed customers named fit inconsistency as their top frustration, according to the Q2 board deck [[SOUTHPEAK/BOARD-DECK@v1:SL8]]. The individual survey rows provided all carry fit_inconsistency as the top pain point, but they appear to be a filtered subset and cannot show the share of the full sample [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R6]][[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R269]].

### Key findings

- 33% of surveyed customers named fit inconsistency as their top frustration [[SOUTHPEAK/BOARD-DECK@v1:SL8]].
- Every survey row provided lists top_pain_point as fit_inconsistency, for example in the 55+ Urban Outdoor and Alpine Committed segments [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R6]][[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R80]].
- Respondent comments cite hiking pants fit changing each season [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R40]], boots and trail runners not matching in size [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R81]], and repeated boot exchanges [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R178]].

### Conflicting evidence

- The nps values differ across respondents, for example 9 in one row and 3 in another [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R6]][[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R277]]. This reflects individual scores, not a disagreement about the fit-inconsistency share, so it does not affect the percentage.

### Interpretation

The survey rows appear to have been selected because they cite fit inconsistency, so they should not be used to estimate the overall share [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The full survey dataset or its methodology summary would close these gaps.

items.question: What share of Southpeak's Urban Outdoor respondents are detractors, meaning they scored 6 or lower?
items.content:
### Answer

The evidence cannot establish a share of detractors among Southpeak's Urban Outdoor respondents, because it contains only 12 individual survey rows, not the full respondent base or any stated share [inference]. Within these 12 rows, two respondents scored 6 or lower: one scored 3 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R119]] and one scored 6 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R147]].

### Key findings

- Respondent SP-R0118 (Urban Outdoor, Backpacking) gave an nps of 3 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R119]].
- Respondent SP-R0146 (Urban Outdoor, Trail running) gave an nps of 6 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R147]].
- The other rows show nps scores of 8 to 10, which are not detractor scores: 9 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R97]], 10 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R171]], 8 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R127]], 10 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R157]], 8 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R159]], 9 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R148]], 9 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R32]], 9 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R64]], 8 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R111]], 9 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R266]].

### Conflicting evidence

- The flagged "conflicts" are only differing NPS scores across individual respondents (for example 9 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R97]] versus 10 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R171]]). These are separate survey answers, not contradictory statements about one metric.

### Interpretation

The two detractors among 12 rows should not be read as the segment's detractor share, because the rows appear to be a selected sample (many share near-identical verbatims) rather than a random or complete draw [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The total number of Urban Outdoor respondents in the survey is not provided. No source states a detractor share or a count of detractors for the segment. The full survey dataset, or a published segment-level NPS breakdown, would close this gap.

items.question: On the 1-to-5 price sensitivity scale, what is the average for survey respondents aged 18 to 27?

- Price sensitivity averaged 3.9 among Gen Z and 3.2 among older customers on a five point scale where five means very sensitive [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P4.B3]].
- The Q3 review restates 3.9 for Gen Z and 3.2 for older customers, from the May survey of 400 Gen Z respondents [[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL6]].

### Interpretation

If Gen Z in this survey corresponds to ages 18 to 27, the 3.9 figure would be the relevant average, but the evidence does not confirm that mapping [inference]. The few individual rows provided are a selected sample of 18-21 respondents and cannot be used to derive a representative average [inference].

items.question: Excluding the total line, which customer age segment does finance expect to grow fastest in FY26?
items.content:
### Answer

Finance expects the Gen Z (18-27) segment to grow fastest in FY26, at 13.8% year over year [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R2]]. The other age segments are projected to grow more slowly, with Millennial (28-43) at 6.2% [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R3]] and Boomer and older (60+) at 6.1% [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R5]].

### Key findings

- Millennial (28-43): yoy_growth_pct of 6.2 [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R3]].
- Boomer and older (60+): yoy_growth_pct of 6.1 [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R5]].
- Gen X (44-59): yoy_growth_pct of 4.4 [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R4]].
- The Total line shows yoy_growth_pct of 7.2 and is excluded from the ranking [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R6]].
- The Gen Z growth of 13.8% is described as roughly double the growth rate of the company overall [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P2.B1]].

### Conflicting evidence

- The segment rows differ in their "definition" field only because each segment covers a different age band, for example Gen Z as customers aged 18 to 27 [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R2]] and Gen X as customers aged 44 to 59 [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R4]]. This is not a disagreement on the growth metric.
- The finance definition of Gen Z (customers aged 18 to 27) differs from the brand team's loyalty program definition, which stretches the age band to 16 through 29 and so gives a higher share [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P2.B1]]. The 13.8% figure is on the finance basis.

### Interpretation

The ranking is unambiguous on the finance basis, since the Gen Z growth rate is well above every other age segment's rate [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

FY26 figures are latest estimates because the year is still open, so the final outcome is not established. Actual full-year results would close this gap. The evidence does not show growth under the brand team's wider age definition. The planned reconciliation bridge between the finance and brand definitions would address this.

### Answer

- A competitor, Kinetic Lab, states delivery in 14 to 21 days from scan approval, which is not a Northstar channel figure [[NORTHSTAR/KINETIC-AR@v1:P3.B4]].

### Conflicting evidence

- The week six early read of 27% repeat purchase was superseded by the full window result [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B12]]. This concerns repeat purchase, not delivery time.
- The two reviews carry different dates, 2026-06-14 and 2025-11-01, but they are separate reviews and this does not affect any delivery figure [[NORTHSTAR/REVIEWS@v1:R49]][[NORTHSTAR/REVIEWS@v1:R683]].

### Gaps & unknowns

No evidence item reports delivery time by sales channel, such as brand site, app, store or marketplace. No numeric average is given for standard orders, only qualitative descriptions. A fulfilment or logistics report with delivery days split by channel and order type would close this gap.

The survey table is described only by its structure (600 rows with price_sensitivity and nps columns), and only two individual rows are quoted; the other evidence reports segment-level averages and NPS scores, not respondent-level data [inference].

- E8 records nps 9 and E10 records nps 10, both with price_sensitivity 4 [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R124]][[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R545]]. These are different respondents, not a disagreement about the same metric, so they do not conflict.

### Interpretation

The direction of the two group-level comparisons (higher price sensitivity alongside lower NPS among Gen Z) is consistent with a negative relationship, but two group averages cannot establish a correlation across individual respondents [inference]. The two sample rows, both with the same price sensitivity score and different NPS values, say nothing about the overall relationship [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

Closing the gap requires the raw survey export, or a published analysis that reports the correlation between price sensitivity and NPS.

items.question: Which four Gen Z customer groups does the brand strategy describe?
items.content:
### Answer

The Northstar Athletics Brand Strategy 2026 divides its Gen Z customer base into four segments: Campus Competitors, Studio Social, Trail Starters and Value Seekers [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B1]].

### Key findings

- Campus Competitors make up 24% of Gen Z and are college and club athletes aged 18 to 22 [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B1]].
- Studio Social is the largest segment at 31% of Gen Z customers, focused on class based fitness and athleisure, with the highest average order value of $94 [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B2]].
- Trail Starters make up 19% of Gen Z and are new runners and hikers going light trail [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B1]].
- Value Seekers make up 26% of Gen Z and are price led shoppers who switch with Pace & Co. [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B1]].
- The segmentation was rebuilt this year from survey responses and order history for use by merchandising, marketing and product [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B1]].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence does not show how segment membership is assigned to individual customers, nor how the segments differ in return behaviour, channel use or lifetime value. Detailed segment profiles from the brand strategy document or the underlying survey data would close these gaps.

items.question: According to the trends report, how do young shoppers weigh peer reviews and creator try-on videos against brand advertising?
items.content:
### Answer

According to the Gen Z Athletic Trends 2026 report, 57% of Gen Z respondents trust peer reviews and creator try-on videos more than brand advertising [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]]. Advertising is treated as a prompt to look rather than a reason to buy [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]]. Shoppers typically check several reviews and at least one video of the product on a real person before purchasing [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].

### Key findings

- 57% of Gen Z respondents said they trust peer reviews and creator try-on videos more than brand advertising [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].
- Reviews that mention fit, sizing across categories and durability after several weeks of wear were rated the most useful [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].
- Shoppers notice when a brand removes or hides critical reviews [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].
- Entry to a shopper's shortlist is driven by peer exposure, prior ownership and visible social proof, while a single bad signal such as a run of poor reviews can cause exit [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P3.B3]].
- The report's implications for brands include publishing reviews openly, since shoppers rely on peers and creators to judge fit and durability [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P5.B1]].
- The report notes that social purchase paths use the video as a try-on and the comment thread as a size guide [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P2.B2]].

### Interpretation

The report's framing suggests peer evidence is a gatekeeper rather than a late-stage persuader: a brand with hidden or weak reviews may be filtered out before the sale [inference]. The 57% figure shows a majority preference, not unanimity, so advertising likely retains some role in prompting initial attention [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence does not give the share of respondents who trust advertising more, or who weigh the two equally. It also does not break trust levels down by segment (for example team athletes versus price-led shoppers) or by region [inference]. The survey sample size and wording of the question are not provided. A look at the report's methodology section or underlying survey tables would close these gaps.

- Another respondent would pick the brand that is honest about its factories, even if it costs a bit more [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R196]].
- A focus group, not a survey segment, found specific facts on recycled proportion, place of manufacture and what happens to a worn pair preferred to badges and slogans [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B4]].

- The only disagreement is in individual nps scores, which vary across respondents (for example 9 in [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R437]] versus 4 in [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R493]]). This is respondent-level variation and does not bear on the question.

### Interpretation

The disclosure demands are consistent across respondents: concrete material, factory and end-of-life facts rather than green labels or icons [inference].

The share of Studio Social respondents with sustainability transparency as their top pain point cannot be derived, because the evidence gives neither the segment's total respondent count nor the full distribution of pain points. A complete tabulation of the survey data by segment and top_pain_point would close this gap. The sampled rows were returned because they match the topic, so they may over-represent this concern and should not be read as a representative share [inference].

### Key findings

- Across the May survey, personalization was named by a small share of respondents as their top frustration; no percentage is given and it is not broken out for Campus Competitors [[NORTHSTAR/FY27-MEMO@v1:S1.B4]].
- Five provided Campus Competitors rows (R0342, R0591, R0595, R0352, R0518) each record top_pain_point as lack_of_personalization [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R343]][[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R592]][[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R596]][[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R353]][[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R519]].

- Saving fit preferences and getting recommendations is requested [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R519]].
